at pakke.explanation: "At pakke" means "to pack", for example a suitcase or a bag: "Jeg pakker min kuffert" (I pack my suitcase). It also means "to wrap": "pakke en gave ind" (to wrap a present). "En pakke" (a parcel) looks the same.

sentence.en: I am packing my suitcase tonight.

at prøve.explanation: "At prøve" means "to try": "Jeg prøver at lære dansk" (I am trying to learn Danish). It also means "to try on", for example "prøve en kjole" (to try on a dress). "En prøve" means "a test" or "a sample".

sentence.en: I am trying to speak Danish.

at prøve tøj.explanation: "At prøve tøj" means "to try on clothes", for example in a shop. To ask about one item, you can say "Må jeg prøve den?" (May I try it on?).

sentence.da: Jeg vil gerne **prøve tøj** i butikken.
sentence.en: I would like to try on clothes in the shop.

en pakke.explanation: "En pakke" means "a package" or "a parcel", and also "a packet", like "en pakke smør" (a packet of butter). You can say "Der er kommet en pakke" (A parcel has arrived). "At pakke" means "to pack".

sentence.da: Der er kommet **en pakke** til dig.
sentence.en: A package has come for you.

en pandekage.explanation: "En pandekage" means "a pancake", built from "pande" (a pan) and "kage" (a cake). A frying pan is "en pande".

sentence.en: My mother makes pancakes on Sundays.

en paraply.explanation: "En paraply" means "an umbrella", said pa-ra-PLY. You often hear "Tag en paraply med" (Take an umbrella with you).

sentence.en: Take an umbrella with you.

en park.explanation: "En park" means "a park". You say "i parken" (in the park). Do not mix it up with "at parkere" (to park a car).

sentence.en: The children are playing in the park.

en patient.explanation: "En patient" means "a patient", a person getting medical care. The spelling matches English, but the "ti" sounds like "tsi", so it says "pa-tsi-ent". Patients are found at "et sygehus" (a hospital) or "en klinik" (a clinic).

sentence.en: The doctor talks with the patient.

en pause.explanation: "En pause" means "a break" or "a pause", for example at work or school. "At holde pause" means "to take a break", and "en kaffepause" (a coffee break) is a short one.

sentence.en: We take a break at ten o'clock.

en pen.explanation: "En pen" means "a pen". Do not mix it up with "pæn" (nice, pretty), which is spelled with an "æ". A ballpoint pen is "en kuglepen" (a ballpoint pen).

sentence.en: I write with a pen.

en perron.explanation: "En perron" means "a platform" at a train station. You will hear "Toget kører fra perron 3" (The train leaves from platform 3). Danish does not use "platform" for this: the word "perron" comes from French.

sentence.en: The train leaves from platform two.

en person.explanation: "En person" means "a person". When booking you say "et bord til to personer" (a table for two people). For people in general, Danes often say "mennesker" (human beings).

sentence.en: There are three people in the car.

en pige.explanation: "En pige" means "a girl". It can also mean "a girlfriend" or "a young woman", but for a grown woman "en kvinde" (a woman) is safer. The matching word is "en dreng" (a boy).

sentence.da: Den lille **pige** har en rød kjole.
sentence.en: The little girl has a red dress.

en pille.explanation: "En pille" means "a pill" or "a tablet". You say "at tage en pille" (to take a pill). "Pillen" (the pill) can also mean the birth control pill.

sentence.da: Tag en **pille** to gange om dagen.
sentence.en: Take one pill twice a day.

en pingvin.explanation: "En pingvin" means "a penguin". Danish spells the sound with "v" ("pingvin"), where English has "gu" ("penguin").

sentence.en: The penguin swims in the water.

en pizza.explanation: "En pizza" means "a pizza". To order one to take away, say "en pizza til at tage med" (a pizza to take with you).

sentence.en: We are ordering a pizza tonight.

en plads.explanation: "En plads" means "a seat", "room" (space) or "a town square". On a train or in a cinema, "en plads" is your seat. "Er der plads?" means "Is there room?" and "Der er ikke mere plads" means "There is no more room".

sentence.en: Is there room for me?

en plan.explanation: "En plan" means "a plan". A common question is "Har du planer i weekenden?" (Do you have plans this weekend?). "At planlægge" means "to plan", and "en køreplan" is a timetable for buses.

sentence.da: Hvad er din **plan** for i dag?
sentence.en: What is your plan for today?

en plastikpose.explanation: "En plastikpose" means "a plastic bag", from "plastik" (plastic) and "en pose" (a bag). In shops you may hear "Vil du have en pose?" (Do you want a bag?).

sentence.en: I need a plastic bag.

en politistation.explanation: "En politistation" means "a police station", built from "politi" (police) and "station" (station). You say "på politistationen" (at the police station).

sentence.en: Where is the police station?

en portion.explanation: "En portion" means "a portion" or "a serving", such as one person's share of food. In restaurants you may hear "en lille portion" (a small portion) or "en stor portion" (a large one). Unlike in English, the stress is at the end: "por-ti-ON".

sentence.en: Can I have a large portion?

en pose.explanation: "En pose" means "a bag", a soft bag of plastic or paper, like the one you get in a shop. A bag you carry, such as a handbag, is "en taske" (a bag, purse). In a shop you may hear "Skal du have en pose?" (Do you want a bag?).

sentence.en: Do you want a bag?

en pris.explanation: "En pris" means "a price", what something costs. The same word also means a prize or award, so the situation tells you which: "en pris på tyve kroner" (a price of twenty crowns) is a price, while "at vinde en pris" (to win a prize) is an award.

sentence.en: What is the price?

en pude.explanation: "En pude" means "a pillow" and also a cushion, for example on a sofa. A bed pillow can be called "en hovedpude" (literally "a head pillow"). At a hotel you can ask "Kan jeg få en ekstra pude?" (Can I have an extra pillow?).

sentence.da: Jeg vil gerne have en ekstra **pude**.
sentence.en: I would like an extra pillow.

en pung.explanation: "En pung" means "a wallet", a small one for coins and notes. "En tegnebog" (a wallet) means almost the same thing, but "pung" is the one you hear in everyday speech: "Jeg har glemt min pung" (I have forgotten my wallet).

sentence.en: Where is my wallet?

en pyjamas.explanation: "En pyjamas" means "a pair of pajamas". Danish treats it as one thing, so you say "en pyjamas" (literally "a pajamas") where English says "a pair of pajamas".

sentence.en: The children are wearing pajamas.

en pære.explanation: "En pære" means "a pear" and also "a light bulb", so the situation tells you which one is meant: "en saftig pære" (a juicy pear) is fruit, while "en ny pære" (a new bulb) is something for a lamp.

sentence.da: Jeg har købt tre **pærer** på markedet.
sentence.en: I bought three pears at the market.

en pølse.explanation: "En pølse" means "a sausage". A hot dog is "en hotdog" or "en pølse i brød" (a sausage in bread), and a street stand that sells them is "en pølsevogn" (a sausage wagon).

sentence.en: I would like a sausage.

et par.explanation: "Et par" means "a pair" or "a couple", as in "et par sko" (a pair of shoes). It also means "a few": "et par dage" means "a couple of days". Two people in a relationship are also "et par".

sentence.en: I will stay here for a couple of days.

et par jeans.explanation: "Et par jeans" means "a pair of jeans". You can also just say "jeans": "Jeg har jeans på" means "I am wearing jeans".

sentence.en: I have bought a pair of jeans.

et pas.explanation: "Et pas" means "a passport", the document you show at the border. "Husk dit pas" means "Remember your passport". Do not mix it up with "at passe" (to fit, to look after), which looks similar.

sentence.en: Do you have your passport?

et plaster.explanation: "Et plaster" means "a band-aid", a small sticky bandage for a cut. "At sætte et plaster på" means "to put a band-aid on".

sentence.en: I need a band-aid.

et postkontor.explanation: "Et postkontor" means "a post office", where you send letters and parcels. It is built from "post" (mail) and "kontor" (office). You may also hear "et posthus" (a post office), which means the same.

sentence.en: When does the post office open?

et postkort.explanation: "Et postkort" means "a postcard". It is built from "post" (mail) and "kort" (card). A common way to start writing one is "Hilsen fra..." (Greetings from...).

sentence.en: I am sending a postcard home.

et problem.explanation: "Et problem" means "a problem". Danes often say "Det er ikke noget problem" (It is no problem) to be relaxed about something. "Hvad er problemet?" means "What is the problem?".

sentence.en: There is a problem with the car.

et prøverum.explanation: "Et prøverum" means "a fitting room", the small room in a clothing shop where you try on clothes. It is built from "at prøve" (to try) and "et rum" (a room).

sentence.en: Where is the fitting room?

forms.en: There is a deposit on the bottle

pant.explanation: "Pant" means "deposit": a small extra amount added to the price of a bottle or can. You get the money back when you return the empty bottle to a machine in the shop.

sentence.en: I am going to return deposit bottles at the shop.

papir.explanation: "Papir" means "paper", the material you write or print on. "Et stykke papir" (a piece of paper) is how you say one sheet. "Papirer" can also mean "documents", such as the papers you show at a border or a hotel.

sentence.da: Jeg har brug for et stykke **papir**.
sentence.en: I need a piece of paper.

pas på.explanation: "Pas på" means "watch out" or "be careful". It can be a warning shouted in an emergency or a calm reminder, like "pas på, det er varmt" (careful, it is hot). It also means "look after": "pas på børnene" is "look after the children".

sentence.en: Watch out, the floor is wet!

forms.da: Pas på dig selv i trafikken.
forms.en: Look after yourself in the traffic.

pas på dig selv.explanation: "Pas på dig selv" means "take care of yourself" and is a warm way to say goodbye. Danes say it to someone going on a trip, feeling ill, or just heading home. To several people, say "pas på jer selv" (take care of yourselves).

sentence.en: Goodbye, and take care of yourself!

pasta.explanation: "Pasta" means "pasta", and it is spelled and said much like in English. Danish leaves out "a" before it, as in "Jeg laver pasta" (I am making pasta).

sentence.en: I am making pasta for dinner.

peber.explanation: "Peber" means "pepper", the spice you put on food. It is used without "a", as in "salt og peber" (salt and pepper). Do not mix it up with "peberfrugt" (bell pepper), which is a vegetable.

sentence.en: I add a little salt and pepper.

penge.explanation: "Penge" means "money". It only comes in the "more than one" form, so there is no "a money". For one coin or one note, say "en mønt" (a coin) or "en seddel" (a banknote).

sentence.en: I do not have a lot of money.

perfekt.explanation: "Perfekt" means "perfect", just like in English. On its own it works as an exclamation: "Perfekt!" means "Great, that works!".

sentence.en: It is the perfect gift.

pludselig.explanation: "Pludselig" means "suddenly" and also "sudden". "Pludselig kom han ind" means "Suddenly he came in". "Lige pludselig" is a bit stronger, like "all of a sudden".

sentence.en: Suddenly it began to rain.

polen.explanation: "Polen" means "Poland". A person from there is "en polak" (a Pole) and the language is "polsk" (Polish). You use "Polen" without "the", like "Poland" in English.

sentence.en: My colleague comes from Poland.

politi.explanation: "Politi" means "police". Danish treats it as one thing, so you say "politiet er her" (the police is here). One officer is "en politibetjent" (a police officer).

sentence.en: The police will come in five minutes.

polsk.explanation: "Polsk" means "Polish", for things from Poland and for the language. Unlike English, it is written with a small letter: "polsk", not "Polsk". A person is "en polak" (a Pole).

sentence.da: Min nabo kommer fra Polen og taler **polsk**.
sentence.en: My neighbour comes from Poland and speaks Polish.

pommes frites.explanation: "Pommes frites" means "French fries", and it is said in a French-like way. Danes often shorten it to "pommes". Burger places ask "vil du have pommes frites til?" (do you want fries with that?).

sentence.da: Jeg vil gerne have **pommes frites** og ketchup.
sentence.en: I would like fries and ketchup.

post.explanation: "Post" means "mail": the letters and parcels that arrive. It is also the word for the postal service. The person who delivers it is "postbudet" (the mail carrier), and the office is "postkontoret" (the post office).

sentence.en: Have you got the mail?

præcis.explanation: "Præcis" means "exactly" or "precisely", and is used for time, amounts and details. On its own, "Præcis!" means "Exactly!" or "That's right!". For a rough amount, use "cirka" (approximately) instead.

sentence.en: The train comes exactly at eight o'clock.

på.explanation: "På" means "on", but also "at" or "in" in many fixed phrases: "på arbejde" (at work), "på ferie" (on holiday), "på dansk" (in Danish). Learn these as whole phrases. It is also used with islands and streets: "på Fyn" (on Funen), "på gaden" (on the street).

sentence.en: The phone is on the table.

på gensyn.explanation: "På gensyn" means "until we see each other again" and is a polite, slightly formal goodbye. It is common in shops, on the phone and at work. With friends, "vi ses" (see you) is more usual.

sentence.en: Thanks for the visit. See you again!

på tilbud.explanation: "På tilbud" means "on sale", with a lower price for a short time. It comes from "et tilbud" (an offer). You see it on shop signs next to the lowered price.

sentence.da: Kaffen er **på tilbud** i denne uge.
sentence.en: The coffee is on sale this week.

forms.en: The bus is on its way.

på vej.explanation: "På vej" means "on the way" and is used for both coming and going. Say "jeg er på vej" when you are travelling toward a place, and add where to, like "på vej til arbejde" (on the way to work). It is very handy in text messages.

sentence.en: I'm on my way to school.

påske.explanation: "Påske" means "Easter". You use it without "a" or "the" in "til påske" (at Easter), but "i påsken" is how you say "during Easter". The greeting is "Glædelig påske!" (Happy Easter!).

sentence.en: We are on holiday at Easter.

pæn.explanation: "Pæn" means "nice-looking", "neat" or "tidy". It is used for people and things that look good in a simple way, for tidy rooms, and for good behaviour: "vær pæn" means "be well-behaved".

sentence.da: Du ser meget **pæn** ud i dag.
sentence.en: You look very nice today.
